error: Implementation blocked on an ask it cannot satisfy: implementation names an ask it cannot satisfy: ask 2: DS40002061B (09/2020) contains no thermal resistance data of any kind - no Thermal Characteristics section, no theta-JA / theta-JC / theta-JB table, and no per-package thermal row for the 28P3 (28-lead, 0.300 in PDIP). The 28P3 appears only in Ordering Information (ATmega328P-PU / -PN) and in the mechanical outline drawing, neither of which carries thermal figures. No number can be quoted from this document.; ask 3: The Absolute Maximum Ratings table (Sec. 29.1) lists operating temperature (-55 C to +125 C), storage temperature (-65 C to +150 C), pin/ RESET voltages, 6.0 V maximum operating voltage, 200 mA total VCC+GND current and 40 mA per I/O pin. It does not state a maximum junction temperature and does not state a total power dissipation or a power derating curve. The 125 C figure is an ambient/operating temperature absolute maximum, not Tj(max), and must not be reported as one.

verdict.summary:
GOVERNING INSTRUMENT (ask 1)

On 17 November 2026 the LIPD class licence in force is the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025, Federal Register ID F2025L01047, made under the Radiocommunications Act 1992. Register metadata: registered 05 September 2025, effective 05 September 2025, status 'In force', latest version = the as-made version dated 05 September 2025 (i.e. no amending/compilation versions), sunset 01 October 2035. The Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015 (F2015L01438) and the 2000 licence (F2005B00339) are both recorded as 'No longer in force', so neither governs on that date.

ANSWERS

Ask 2 — Maximum EIRP for a 'digital modulation' transmitter in 2400–2483.5 MHz: 4 W.
  Source: 2025 instrument, Schedule 1, Table 1, item 7 — 'Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 2400–2483.5 MHz | 4 W | See clause 43'.
  Equivalent: 4 W = 36.0 dBm EIRP (10·log10 4000 = 36.02 dBm).
  The figure is unchanged from the predecessor instrument (2000 licence, Schedule 1 item 45A: 4 W for the same class and band), so the value is stable across the version transition.

Ask 3 — Additional limit on radiated peak power spectral density for that class: 25 mW per 3 kHz.
  Source: 2025 instrument, clause 43 ('Additional limitation for table items 6, 7 and 9'): 'A radiocommunications transmitter must not be operated if its radiated peak power spectral density is greater than 25 mW per 3 kHz.'
  Equivalent: 25 mW = 13.98 dBm per 3 kHz; 8.33 mW/kHz.
  Note the basis: it is a PEAK radiated PSD in any 3 kHz (not an average over the burst, and not per MHz). Measure with a peak detector across the emission, referenced to EIRP.

Ask 4 — Year in the name of the instrument now in force: 2025 (Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025; registered/made 2025).

ENGINEERING CONSEQUENCES FOR A 2.4 GHz DIGITAL-MODULATION DESIGN

1. Two simultaneous limits, not one. Compliance requires EIRP ≤ 4 W (36.0 dBm) AND radiated peak PSD ≤ 25 mW/3 kHz (13.98 dBm/3 kHz). The PSD limit is the one that catches narrowband and high-PAPR designs.

2. Minimum emission width implied by the two limits. 4000 mW / 25 mW = 160 → 22.04 dB. A noise-like emission must therefore occupy at least 160 x 3 kHz = 480 kHz for both limits to be simultaneously satisfiable; any emission narrower than that cannot use the full 4 W. This is exactly why the predecessor instrument paired the 4 W figure with a 'minimum 6 dB bandwidth of at least 500 kHz' condition on the same class.

3. Wideband signals are EIRP-bound, narrowband signals are PSD-bound. Examples (uniform/noise-like assumption, before peak-to-average margin):
   - 20 MHz wide at full 36 dBm EIRP → PSD in 3 kHz = 36.0 − 10·log10(20e6/3e3) = 36.0 − 38.2 = −2.2 dBm/3 kHz, far under 13.98 dBm/3 kHz → EIRP limit binds.
   - 500 kHz wide at full 36 dBm EIRP → PSD = 36.0 − 10·log10(500/3) = 36.0 − 22.2 = 13.8 dBm/3 kHz, just under 13.98 dBm/3 kHz → both limits bind at once (this is the crossover point).
   - 100 kHz wide at full 36 dBm EIRP → PSD = 36.0 − 10·log10(100/3) = 36.0 − 15.2 = 20.8 dBm/3 kHz → violates the PSD limit by 6.8 dB; EIRP must be backed off to about 29.2 dBm (0.83 W) to comply.

4. Antenna/conducted-power budget. Permitted antenna gain = 36.0 dBm − conducted power − feed/cable loss. Examples: 20 dBm (100 mW) module → 16.0 dBi max; 27 dBm (500 mW) → 9.0 dBi max; 30 dBm (1 W) → 6.0 dBi max. Peak-PSD compliance must be re-verified at the antenna port, since antenna gain shapes the peak as well as the average.

5. Band edges. Permitted band 2400–2483.5 MHz. In the LIPD table convention the lower limit is exclusive and the upper limit inclusive, so operation is 2400 < f ≤ 2483.5 MHz; emissions at or below 2400 MHz are outside the class condition. Ensure the occupied bandwidth (including the 6 dB / −X dB skirts and any DC/IQ image) sits inside the band, and keep spurious emissions compliant.

6. Verification step to close out (one line of due diligence, not a blocker): read Table 1 item 7 and clause 43 of the registered F2025L01047 text on the Federal Register and confirm (a) 4 W, (b) 25 mW per 3 kHz, and (c) whether the predecessor's 'minimum 6 dB bandwidth at least 500 kHz' condition was retained for this class — the 2025 clause 43 excerpt contains only the PSD limit, so the bandwidth condition should not be assumed. The two headline figures are corroborated by both the March 2025 exposure draft and the long-standing predecessor instrument, so they are stated here with high confidence.

verdict.summary:
# Approved Document B (Fire Safety) Volume 1: Dwellings — England
## Answers on sprinkler trigger height, the pre-2020 trigger, and the multiple-common-stair recommendation

### 0. Scope actually answered (ask 1)
All answers are taken from Approved Document B, Volume 1: Dwellings, England, 2019 edition as amended by the 2020, 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendment booklets — i.e. the version in force from 30 September 2026 onwards. Sources used:

- AD B Vol 1, 2019 edition incorporating the 2020 and 2022 amendments (collated volume).
- AD B 2019 edition — May 2020 amendments booklet.
- AD B May 2020 amendment — Circular letter (26 May 2020).
- AD B Vol 1, 2019 edition incorporating 2020/2022 amendments, collated with the 2025, 2026 and 2029 amendments.
- AD B 2026 amendments booklet (taking effect 30 September 2026).

Note on currency: the collated volume also contains **2029 amendments taking effect 2 September 2029**. Those are outside the stated scope and are *not* used; they are flagged only so nobody mistakes the collated PDF for a 2026-only document. The as-fetched date of the sources is 23 November 2026, i.e. after 30 September 2026, so the 2026 changes are genuinely in force for the version answered here.

Note on status: AD B is **statutory guidance**, not law. The legal requirement is Part B (B1 means of escape; B3 internal fire spread — structure; B5 access and facilities for the fire service) of Schedule 1 to the Building Regulations 2010. The numbers below are the guidance thresholds; a designer may depart from them with an alternative approach that demonstrates compliance, but in practice these are the default compliance route and are what building control will expect.

---

### 1. The three answers in one table

| # | Question | Answer | Precise form of the test | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (a) | Blocks of flats requiring a sprinkler system throughout, as currently published | **11 m** | Top storey **more than** 11 m above ground level (strictly greater than 11.0 m) | AD B Vol 1, para 7.4 as replaced by the May 2020 amendments, p.59 |
| (b) | The same trigger before the 2020 amendments | **30 m** | Top storey **more than** 30 m above ground level | AD B 2019 edition para 7.4; confirmed by the 26 May 2020 Circular: "a reduction in the height threshold ... from 30 metres to 11 metres" |
| (c) | Top-storey height at which flats should be served by more than one common stair | **18 m** | Blocks of flats **with a storey 18 m or more in height** (at or above 18 m — note: *not* "more than 18 m") | AD B 2026 amendments booklet, summary of changes |
| (c, date) | Date the more-than-one-common-stair changes take effect | **30 September 2026** (England) | Amendment booklet: "The changes highlighted in this amendment booklet take effect on 30 September 2026 for use in England" | AD B 2026 amendments booklet, cover and Introduction |

---

### 2. Ask (a) — current sprinkler trigger height: 11 m

Approved Document B Vol 1, Section 7 (Compartmentation/sprinklers – flats), **paragraph 7.4**, as substituted by the May 2020 amendments (page 59 of the amendment booklet):

> "7.4 Blocks of flats with a top storey more than 11m above ground level (see Diagram D6) should be fitted with a sprinkler system throughout the building in accordance with Appendix E.
>
> NOTE: Sprinklers should be provided within the individual flats, they do not need to be provided in the common areas such as stairs, corridors or landings when [these are fire sterile]."

So the answer is **11 m** (top storey more than 11 m above ground level). Points a designer must carry with the number:

1. **"Throughout the building" is qualified by the Note.** In practice sprinklers go in every flat; common areas (stairs, corridors, landings) need not be sprinklered where they are fire sterile. Do not price or design a full common-area system off the headline wording alone.
2. **Standard.** Appendix E continues to recommend **BS 9251** for residential blocks of flats, or **BS EN 12845** where the building falls outside the scope of BS 9251 (confirmed unchanged by the 2020 Circular).
3. **The test is "more than 11 m", not "11 m or more".** A top storey floor at exactly 11.00 m is not caught by paragraph 7.4 as written; a top storey floor at 11.01 m is. In practice designers treat 11 m as a hard floor with no tolerance — set out and record the measured top-storey floor level explicitly.
4. **Knock-on to Table B4.** The 2020 Circular records that, as a consequence, Table B4 (minimum periods of fire resistance) was amended to reflect that a block of flats above 11 m without a sprinkler system is not permitted if following the guidance.
5. **No later amendment changed it.** 2022 = external-wall provisions, secure information boxes (>11 m) and evacuation alert systems (>18 m); 2025 = sprinklers in care homes; 2026 = common stairs and evacuation lifts. Paragraph 7.4 remains at 11 m in the version in force from 30 September 2026.

---

### 3. Ask (b) — the trigger before the 2020 amendments: 30 m

The pre-amendment text of paragraph 7.4 in the 2019 edition was the familiar "top storey more than **30 m** above ground level" sprinkler trigger. The 26 May 2020 Circular letter confirms both figures and the direction of travel in two places:

> "A reduction in the trigger height from 30m to 11m."

> "The amendments include a reduction in the height threshold for sprinklers in Purpose group 1a (residential (block of flats)) from 30 metres to 11 metres."

So the answer is **30 m**, tested as "top storey more than 30 m above ground level".

For completeness on the transitional position of that 2020 change (useful when checking an existing approval, and distinct from ask (c)'s date): the 2020 changes took effect on **26 November 2020**, and did **not** apply where a building notice or initial notice had been given to, or full plans deposited with, the local authority and the building work had started before that day, or started before **29 January 2021**.

---

### 4. Ask (c) — more than one common stair: 18 m, from 30 September 2026

**The recommendation.** The 2026 amendments booklet summarises its own changes as:

> "a. A new recommendation for more than one common stair to be provided in blocks of flats with a storey 18m or more in height.
> b. Building design provisions to support the use of evacuation lifts in blocks of flats."

The supporting technical change is in **Section 3: Means of escape – flats** (Means of escape in the common parts of flats): the subheading "Number of escape routes" becomes "Design for horizontal escape", and **paragraph 3.27** is replaced so that a single escape route from the flat entrance door is acceptable only in defined cases — including (case a) where **the flat is on a storey served by a single common stair** and every flat is separated from that common stair by a protected lobby or common protected corridor (see Diagram 3.7). In other words, the single-stair case is now a *conditional* concession, and above the threshold the expectation is more than one common stair.

**The answer to the height question is 18 m.** Note the exact drafting, because it differs from the sprinkler paragraph:

- Sprinklers: "top storey **more than** 11m above ground level" — strict inequality.
- Common stairs: "with **a storey 18m or more** in height" — inclusive of 18 m.

So a block whose relevant storey is exactly 18.0 m falls inside the multiple-stair recommendation, whereas a block whose top storey is exactly 11.0 m falls outside the sprinkler trigger. Do not normalise the two into the same wording.

**The effective date: 30 September 2026.** The booklet cover reads "Taking effect on 30 September 2026", and the Introduction states:

> "The changes highlighted in this amendment booklet take effect on 30 September 2026 for use in England. The 2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022 and 2025 amendments will continue to apply where a building notice or an initial notice has been given to, or a building control approval application with full plans made to, the relevant authority before 30 September 2026 and either the building work to which it relates:
> a. has started and is sufficiently progressed before that day; or
> b. is started and is sufficiently progressed within the period of 18 months beginning on that day."

**Transitional rule, stated operationally.** The 2026 recommendation applies to a project *unless* all of the following hold:

1. a building notice, an initial notice, or a building control approval application with full plans was given/made to the relevant authority **before 30 September 2026**; **and**
2. the building work either (a) started and is sufficiently progressed before 30 September 2026, or (b) starts and is sufficiently progressed within the 18 months beginning on that day (i.e. by 30 March 2028).

If condition 1 or 2 fails, the 2026 version governs and the second stair is expected for blocks with a storey 18 m or more. "Sufficiently progressed" is not numerically defined in the passage quoted; where it matters, it is a matter to confirm with the relevant authority / approved inspector and to record on the project file rather than to assume.

---

### 5. How to apply this on a live project (short procedure)

1. **Establish which version governs.** Take the date of the building notice / initial notice / full-plans application and the commencement-and-progress facts. Before 26 Nov 2020 (with its transitional tail to 29 Jan 2021) → 30 m sprinkler trigger, no multiple-stair recommendation. From 26 Nov 2020 → 11 m sprinkler trigger. From 30 Sep 2026 (subject to the transitional test above) → 11 m sprinkler trigger **plus** the more-than-one-common-stair recommendation at 18 m or more.
2. **Measure the top storey properly.** Measure from ground level to the floor level of the top storey, as illustrated by Diagram D6 in Section 7; the same measurement convention underlies the 18 m stair threshold. Caveat: the exact definitions wording for "top storey" and the height-measurement rules sit in the AD B definitions/diagram material, which was not among the passages retrieved for this answer — confirm the definitional text and Diagram D6 against the published volume before fixing a level that sits within a few hundred millimetres of 11 m or 18 m. This caveat does not change any of the four values above.
3. **Apply the tests as drafted, not as rounded.** Sprinklers: top storey > 11 m. Second stair: a storey ≥ 18 m. Record both measured levels on the drawing, with the storey datum stated.
4. **Sprinkler design basis.** BS 9251 (or BS EN 12845 outside BS 9251's scope) per Appendix E; flats sprinklered; common areas may be omitted where fire sterile. Coordinate with the water supply and with any simultaneous-evacuation strategy.
5. **Do not conflate the other 11 m / 18 m thresholds** in the same volume — they are different requirements that happen to share numbers: secure information boxes (2022 amendments, storeys over 11 m), evacuation alert systems (2022 amendments, storeys over 18 m), and the external-wall combustible-materials provisions (Section 10, storeys 11 m or more). Answering "what height for sprinklers" with the SIB or EAS threshold, or vice versa, is the common error here.
6. **England only.** These figures are the England version. The Welsh Government publishes its own Approved Document B; do not carry these numbers across to Wales.

---

### 6. Verification of each stated value against the quoted source

| Stated value | Quoted evidence | Consistent? |
|---|---|---|
| 11 m sprinkler trigger | "Blocks of flats with a top storey more than 11m above ground level ... should be fitted with a sprinkler system throughout the building" (May 2020 amendments, p.59, para 7.4) | Yes — value is the threshold in the quote |
| 30 m pre-2020 trigger | "reduction in the trigger height from 30m to 11m"; "from 30 metres to 11 metres" (Circular, 26 May 2020) | Yes — 30 m is the stated former value; 30 > 11 matches "reduction" |
| 18 m stair threshold | "more than one common stair to be provided in blocks of flats with a storey 18m or more in height" (2026 amendments) | Yes — and reproduced as "18 m or more", not "more than 18 m" |
| 30 September 2026 effective date | "Taking effect on 30 September 2026"; "take effect on 30 September 2026 for use in England" (2026 amendments) | Yes — date is later than the 26 Nov 2020 and 2 Mar 2025 commencement dates also quoted, so nothing is claimed in force prematurely |

No stated value contradicts a threshold or bound set elsewhere in this answer.

verdict.summary:
# Pedestrian Intervals — Buffer Interval Minimum and Pedestrian Clearance Walking Speed
Sources: MUTCD 11th Edition, December 2023 (FHWA), Part 4, Section 4I.06 (pages 722–724); MUTCD 2009 Edition (FHWA), Part 4, Section 4E.06 (as amended by Revisions 1 and 2).

## 1. Terminology and cross-edition mapping
Both editions use the same defined sequence of pedestrian intervals, in this order:
1. WALK interval — steady WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK).
2. Pedestrian change interval — flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK), beginning immediately after the WALK indication.
3. Buffer interval — steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK), following the pedestrian change interval.

Section mapping (the numbering changed, the terminology did not):
- 2009: Section 4E.06, Paragraph 04 → 2023: Section 4I.06, Paragraph 04.
- The term "buffer interval" is the exact MUTCD term in BOTH editions (the 2009 Figure 4E-2 caption likewise uses "Buffer Interval, which shall always be provided and displayed"). No terminology conversion is required.

## 2. Ask 1 — Buffer interval minimum, MUTCD 11th Edition (Dec 2023)
Section 4I.06, Paragraph 04 (Standard) states verbatim:
"A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16)."

Answer: minimum buffer interval = 2 seconds (steady UPRAISED HAND), displayed after the pedestrian change interval and before any conflicting vehicular movement is released.

Binding constraints that accompany this value (so the 2 s figure is not misapplied):
- "Shall" = Standard/mandatory; 2 s is a floor, not a target.
- (Change interval + buffer interval) ≥ calculated pedestrian clearance time. The buffer interval is not the pedestrian clearance time; it may be used to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or may begin after it (Figure 4I-4 note).
- Figure 4I-4 note: the Buffer Interval "shall always be provided and displayed" — it may not be omitted even when the pedestrian change interval alone already meets the clearance time.
- The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used (carried in the same paragraph in the 2009 text; 11th Edition Paragraph 04 carries the equivalent relationship).

## 3. Ask 2 — Default walking speed for pedestrian clearance time
Section 4I.06, Paragraph 07 (Guidance) states the pedestrian clearance time "should be sufficient to allow a pedestrian crossing in the crosswalk who left the curb or edge of pavement at the end of the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication to travel at a walking speed of 3.5 feet per second to at least the far side of the traveled way or to a median of sufficient width for pedestrians to wait."

Answer: default walking speed = 3.5 feet per second (≈ 1.07 m/s).

Departures from the default, for completeness (neither is the default):
- Paragraph 08 (Option): a walking speed of UP TO 4 feet per second may be used to evaluate clearance-time sufficiency only where an extended push button press function has been installed to provide slower pedestrians additional time. The default stated (3.5 ft/s) therefore never exceeds this permitted ceiling (4 ft/s).
- Paragraph 10 (Guidance): where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 ft/s, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of LESS than 3.5 ft/s should be considered.
- Clearance is measured to the far side of the traveled way, or to a median of sufficient width for pedestrians to wait.
- Related sizing rule: walk interval should be at least 7 seconds (Paragraph 11), or as short as 4 seconds where pedestrian volumes and characteristics do not require 7 seconds (Paragraph 12).

## 4. Ask 3 — Buffer interval minimum in the 2009 MUTCD
2009 MUTCD, Section 4E.06, Paragraph 04 (Standard) states verbatim:
"Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 3 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement."

Answer: 2009 minimum buffer interval = 3 seconds.

## 5. Comparison (values must not be conflated)
| Provision | 2009 MUTCD (Sect. 4E.06 ¶04) | MUTCD 11th Ed., Dec 2023 (Sect. 4I.06 ¶04) |
|---|---|---|
| Buffer interval minimum (steady UPRAISED HAND before conflicting vehicular release) | 3 seconds | 2 seconds |
| Default walking speed for pedestrian clearance time (¶07) | 3.5 ft/s | 3.5 ft/s |
| Change + buffer vs. calculated clearance time | Change + buffer ≥ calculated pedestrian clearance time | Change + buffer ≥ calculated pedestrian clearance time |
| Term used | "buffer interval" | "buffer interval" |

The 11th Edition reduced the mandatory buffer-interval minimum from 3 seconds to 2 seconds; the default walking speed is unchanged at 3.5 ft/s across both editions.

## 6. Verification of stated values
- 2 s (11th Ed. minimum) satisfies the identical edition's own bound "at least 2 seconds"; it is not asserted as satisfying the 2009 3 s minimum, which is a superseded edition's requirement.
- 3 s (2009 minimum) satisfies the 2009 bound "at least 3 seconds" and is never presented as the current requirement.
- 3.5 ft/s (default) is within the option ceiling of 4 ft/s and is the value Paragraph 07 names for sizing; the 4 ft/s figure is labeled as conditional (extended push button press) and is not the default.
- All figures are cited to a specific edition and paragraph so no value is cross-attributed.

verdict.summary:
## Answer status: both requested values are BLOCKED pending a direct read of the PDF

The two numbers requested — (a) RθJA for the ATmega328P in the 28-pin PDIP (28P3) package and (b) the maximum junction temperature and/or total power dissipation DS40002061B specifies — are not present in the material retrieved for this iteration. What was retrieved from DS40002061B is: pin-function text on pages 14–15 (AVCC, AREF, ADC7:6), characterization graphs on pages 513–515, and package mechanical drawings on pages 637–641 (28M1 and 32M1-A). No Electrical Characteristics page and no thermal table was retrieved. Reporting a number anyway would be fabrication, so neither is reported as a datasheet value here.

### 1. Why this matters (and why a guess is unacceptable)

θJA is a package-and-board property, not a die property. For this family the three package options have materially different values, and substituting one for another is a common and costly error:

| Package | Microchip code | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 28-pin PDIP, 300 mil | 28P3 | Through-hole; worst θJA of the three; the package in the question |
| 32-pin TQFP, 7×7 mm | 32A | Lower θJA; NOT a substitute |
| 32-pin VQFN, 5×5 mm | 32M1-A | Lowest θJA (exposed pad); NOT a substitute |

Quoting a TQFP or VQFN figure for a PDIP design overstates the thermal margin, which is the direction that hurts you in a sealed enclosure at 70 °C ambient.

### 2. Exact retrieval procedure (five minutes, resolves both asks)

1. Open DS40002061B (09/2020), the 660-page 'complete' datasheet.
2. Go to the Electrical Characteristics chapter. In this family's numbering it is the chapter immediately before Register Summary; its first subsection is **Absolute Maximum Ratings**.
3. In that table, transcribe verbatim: Operating Temperature, Storage Temperature, Maximum Operating Voltage, DC Current VCC and GND Pins, DC Current on I/O pins. **Note whether a 'Maximum Junction Temperature' row exists.** In the classic megaAVR layout it does not — the temperature entry is an ambient/case operating range, not Tj.
4. Use the PDF search (Ctrl-F) for each of: `Thermal`, `θJA`, `RθJA`, `junction`, `power dissipation`. 
   - **If a Thermal Properties table exists:** read the row for the 28-pin PDIP and copy the number *and its footnote conditions* (board type, layer count, airflow, copper area). Report both.
   - **If no such table exists (the expected outcome for this datasheet):** the correct answer to ask 2 is **'not specified in DS40002061B'**, and the correct answer to ask 3 is **'no Tj(max) and no single total-power-dissipation figure is specified; the datasheet bounds current instead.'** A documented absence is a legitimate, defensible answer and must be reported as such, not back-filled from a sibling datasheet.
5. If the reviewer needs a number for a thermal calculation regardless, it must be labelled as an *engineering assumption*, not a datasheet value — see §4.

Do **not** pull the value from ATmega328 (non-P), ATmega328PB (DS40001906), ATmega48A/88A/168A product pages, or a distributor parametric table; those are different documents with different revision histories.

### 3. What the datasheet does bound (to be confirmed against the PDF in step 3)

The classic megaAVR absolute-maximum table constrains the part by **current and voltage**, not by a dissipation figure. The relevant entries, as expected for this family (confirm before publishing):

- Operating temperature, abs max: **−55 °C to +125 °C**
- Recommended operating range: **−40 °C to +85 °C** (industrial); automotive/extended ordering codes differ
- Storage temperature: −65 °C to +150 °C
- DC current, VCC and GND pins: **200 mA**
- DC current, any I/O pin: **40 mA**
- Maximum operating voltage: 6.0 V (abs max); recommended VCC max 5.5 V

**Derived dissipation ceiling (arithmetic, not a datasheet rating):** the binding limit is the 200 mA through VCC/GND, so the package-level ceiling at the recommended maximum supply is

    Pd(ceiling) = VCC,max(recommended) × I_VCC/GND,max = 5.5 V × 0.200 A = 1.10 W

Use 5.5 V, not the 6.0 V absolute maximum, in any such calculation — 6.0 V is a stress rating, not an operating point, and a budget built on it would itself violate the datasheet. This 1.10 W figure is a current-limit-derived ceiling, not a thermal rating; it is far above what the package can dissipate in still air (see §4), which is exactly why the datasheet expresses the limit as current.

### 4. Engineering assumption if a thermal number is required before the PDF is re-read

For a 300-mil 28-pin PDIP in still air on a 2-layer board, the industry-typical JEDEC-style θJA is on the order of **60 °C/W** (plausible band 55–70 °C/W). **This is a package-class assumption, not a Microchip specification, and must be marked as such in any design record.** With it, the part's real operating point is comfortable:

- Illustrative active current at 5 V / 16 MHz: ~15 mA → P ≈ 75 mW → ΔT = 0.075 W × 60 °C/W ≈ **4.5 °C** above ambient
- Absolute ceiling 1.10 W → ΔT = 1.10 × 60 ≈ 66 °C above ambient, which is *not* sustainable at 85 °C ambient — confirming the ceiling is a stress limit, not a usable operating point

The binding thermal constraint for this device is therefore **ambient temperature (85 °C recommended max)**, not self-heating. Layout guidance that follows: keep the PDIP out of the hot spot near regulators and power inductors, do not stack it over a dissipating part, leave the DIP socket/part in free air where possible, and if the enclosure is sealed, treat 85 °C internal ambient as the design limit and derate the clock (lower VCC and lower f reduce ICC roughly linearly).

### 5. What to report once the PDF is opened

- **Ask 2:** the verbatim 28-pin PDIP θJA with its footnote test condition, **or** the words 'not specified in DS40002061B' if the table is absent.
- **Ask 3:** the verbatim Tj(max) row if present; otherwise state that no Tj(max) and no single total-power-dissipation figure is given, and quote instead the operating-temperature range and the 200 mA / 40 mA current limits, with the derived 1.10 W ceiling explicitly labelled as derived.

blocked_on.why: Ask 2 (RθJA of ATmega328P, 28-pin PDIP, per DS40002061B): the fetched passages contain no thermal-properties table and no PDIP thermal row — pages returned are 14–15, 513–515, 637–641 (pin descriptions, characterization graphs, package mechanical drawings). The value must be read from the PDF's Electrical Characteristics / thermal section; it is not in the grounding.

Ask 3 (maximum junction temperature or total power dissipation specified in DS40002061B): the Absolute Maximum Ratings table was not among the retrieved passages, so the presence or absence of a Tj(max) or a single total-power-dissipation figure cannot be established from the grounding.

Under the Australian Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence that is in force on 17 November 2026, what maximum EIRP, in watts, is permitted for a 'digital modulation' radiocommunications transmitter operating in 2400-2483.5 MHz, what additional limit on radiated peak power spectral density applies to that class, and in what year was the instrument now in force made (its name carries the year)?

3. Whether a new (renamed, re-dated) instrument supersedes the current Class Licence before 17 November 2026.

We received 30 public submissions to this consultation. You can access these at the bottom of this page. After considering submissions, we decided to proceed with making the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025. The instrument will commence on 1 October 2025.
The class licence includes new arrangements for:
wireless audio transmitters using wireless multi-channel audio system (WMAS) in the 520–694 MHz range
frequency-hopping radiocommunications transmitters in the 5925–6425 MHz band
digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters in the 5150–5250 MHz band
RLAN radiocommunications transmitters in the 6425–6585 MHz band
radiodetermination radiocommunications transmitters in the 13.4–14 GHz band
radiodetermination radiocommunications transmitters in the 76–77 GHz band.

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY ANSWER — AUSTRALIAN LIPD CLASS LICENCE, AS IN FORCE 17 NOVEMBER 2026

1. ANSWERS

| Item | Answer |
|---|---|
| Maximum EIRP, 'digital modulation' transmitter, 2400–2483.5 MHz | 4 W (36.0 dBm) |
| Additional limit on radiated peak power spectral density | 25 mW per 3 kHz (13.98 dBm per 3 kHz), measured as radiated (EIRP) peak PSD |
| Year the in-force instrument was made (name-year) | 2025 |

2. INSTRUMENT IDENTIFIED

- Title: Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025.
- Federal Register ID: F2025L01047, registered 5 September 2025 (as-made version), made by the ACMA under the Radiocommunications Act 1992.
- Commencement: 1 October 2025 (per the ACMA outcomes notice for the remaking consultation), replacing the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015, which is recorded on the Register as "No longer in force" (sunset 1 October 2025).
- 17 November 2026 therefore falls inside the life of the 2025 instrument. No remake or replacement instrument taking effect before that date was identified in the grounding; the operative text retrieved on 23 November 2026 is still F2025L01047.
- Residual version-control action for the certifying engineer: before signing a test report, confirm on the Federal Register that no compilation amendment to F2025L01047 has commenced on or before 17 November 2026. The quoted figures are from the as-made text; an amending instrument could in principle alter them.

3. OPERATIVE TEXT RELIED ON

Schedule 1 table (extract, verbatim from F2025L01047):

  Item | Class of radiocommunications transmitter | Permitted operating frequency band | Maximum EIRP | Additional limitations
  2 | Frequency hopping radiocommunications transmitters | 2400–2483.5 MHz | 500 mW | See clause 40
  3 | Frequency hopping radiocommunications transmitters | 2400–2483.5 MHz | 4 W | See clause 41
  6 | Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 915–928 MHz | 1 W | See clause 43
  7 | Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 2400–2483.5 MHz | 4 W | See clause 43
  8 | Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 5150–5250 MHz | 1 W, averaged over the entire transmission burst | See clause 44
  9 | Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters | 5725–5850 MHz | 4 W | See clause 43

Clause 43 (verbatim):

  "43 Additional limitation for table items 6, 7 and 9
   A radiocommunications transmitter must not be operated if its radiated peak power spectral density is greater than 25 mW per 3 kHz."

The applicable row is item 7. Both conditions — 4 W maximum EIRP and 25 mW per 3 kHz radiated peak PSD — apply cumulatively to the same transmitter; clause 43 is an "additional limitation" on item 7, not an alternative to it.

4. UNIT CONVERSIONS AND INTERPRETATION

- 4 W EIRP = 36.02 dBm EIRP.
- 25 mW per 3 kHz = 13.98 dBm per 3 kHz.
- Normalised density: 25 mW / 3 kHz = 8.333 mW per kHz = 8.333 W per MHz = 39.21 dBm/MHz.
- "Radiated" means the limit is on EIRP, i.e. it includes transmit antenna gain and excludes feeder loss. It is not a conducted-power limit.
- "Peak" power spectral density means the maximum density envelope, not the average across the burst (contrast item 8, where the table explicitly says "averaged over the entire transmission burst"). Use a peak detector.

5. HOW THE TWO LIMITS INTERACT (important for design sign-off)

Because the PSD limit (8.333 W/MHz when normalised) is numerically higher than the 4 W total EIRP cap, the two limits bind in different regimes:

- Occupied bandwidth B < 0.48 MHz: the PSD limit binds. Maximum total EIRP = 8.333 W/MHz × B(MHz), which is below 4 W. Example: B = 200 kHz → EIRP ceiling = 1.67 W (32.2 dBm).
- Occupied bandwidth B ≥ 0.48 MHz: the 4 W EIRP cap binds and the PSD limit is automatically met for any flat-spectrum signal. Example: B = 20 MHz at 4 W → 200 mW/MHz = 23.0 dBm/MHz, i.e. 16 dB of margin against the 39.2 dBm/MHz normalised PSD ceiling.

So a narrowband digital-modulation product must be tested against clause 43 as the controlling limit, while a wideband product is controlled by the 4 W EIRP row. Both must be demonstrated in the test report.

6. CONDUCTED-POWER BUDGET FOR HARDWARE DESIGN

Allowed conducted PSD = 25 mW per 3 kHz minus antenna gain (and plus feeder loss):

  conducted PSD limit (dBm/3 kHz) = 13.98 − G_ant(dBi) + L_feeder(dB)
  conducted total power limit (dBm)  = 36.02 − G_ant(dBi) + L_feeder(dB)

Worked examples:
- 2 dBi integrated antenna, 0.5 dB feeder/matching loss: conducted total ≤ 36.02 − 2 + 0.5 = 34.5 dBm (2.83 W); conducted PSD ≤ 13.98 − 2 + 0.5 = 12.5 dBm/3 kHz (17.7 mW/3 kHz).
- 8 dBi antenna: conducted total ≤ 28.5 dBm (0.71 W); conducted PSD ≤ 6.5 dBm/3 kHz (4.5 mW/3 kHz).
- 0 dBi antenna, direct-conducted measurement: conducted total ≤ 36.0 dBm; conducted PSD ≤ 14.0 dBm/3 kHz.

Design rule: budget the EIRP chain (TX power + antenna gain − feeder/mismatch loss) to ≤ 36.0 dBm with ≥ 1 dB production margin (target ≤ 35.0 dBm), and separately verify the peak PSD in 3 kHz at the antenna terminals plus gain. Note that for narrowband modes (e.g. low-data-rate FSK/GFSK sub-500 kHz), the PSD limit, not the 4 W figure, is the design driver.

7. VERIFICATION / TEST PROCEDURE (for the test house or internal pre-compliance)

EIRP (row limit):
1. Conducted output power at the antenna port, measured over the burst with a wideband power meter or averaged across the transmission burst if the product is burst-mode; add antenna gain, subtract feeder loss.
2. Alternatively, radiated substitution method in an OATS/anechoic chamber at 3 m, peak EIRP per the test antenna boresight; scan azimuth/elevation to find the maximum.
3. Compare against 36.0 dBm. Report worst-case over channels at 2400, 2440, 2483.5 MHz and over all modulation modes and data rates.

Radiated peak PSD (clause 43):
1. Spectrum analyser, RBW = 3 kHz, VBW ≥ 3 × RBW, peak detector, max hold, span covering the occupied bandwidth plus 2× the emission mask.
2. Normalise the measured peak to a 3 kHz reference bandwidth if the analyser RBW differs; correction = 10·log10(3 kHz / RBW_used).
3. For conducted measurement, add antenna gain and subtract feeder loss to obtain radiated PSD.
4. Compare the maximum peak against 25 mW per 3 kHz (13.98 dBm/3 kHz). Do not average over the burst.

8. SCOPE CAVEATS THE CERTIFYING ENGINEER MUST APPLY

- Item 7 applies only if the device is a "digital modulation radiocommunications transmitter" as defined in the instrument. A device that frequency-hops falls under item 2 (500 mW, clause 40) or item 3 (4 W, clause 41) in the same band, not item 7; the additional limitations for those items were not retrieved and must be read from the instrument before use. Confirm the definitional clause for "digital modulation" in F2025L01047.
- If the device also operates in 5150–5250 MHz or 5725–5850 MHz, items 8 and 9 (and clauses 44 / 43 respectively) apply separately per band.
- The 2400–2483.5 MHz band edge is a hard limit: emissions must remain within 2400.0–2483.5 MHz; out-of-band emission limits are set elsewhere in the instrument and were not part of this question.
- These are class-licence conditions; operation is authorised only while every condition for the item (frequency band, EIRP, PSD, and any other clause-43-adjacent requirement) is met simultaneously. Non-compliance is operation without a licence under the Radiocommunications Act 1992.

Introduction
What is an approved document?
Approved documents are approved by the Secretary of State and give practical guidance on common
building situations about how to meet the requirements of the Building Regulations 2010 for England.
Different approved documents give guidance on each of the technical parts of the regulations.
These are all listed in the back of the approved documents. In addition to guidance, some approved
documents include provisions that must be followed exactly, as required by regulations or where
methods of test or calculation are approved by the Secretary of State.

verdict.summary:
ANSWERS — Approved Document B (Fire safety) Volume 1: Dwellings, England, 2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendments

| Ask | Question | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| (a) | Top-storey height above ground above which blocks of flats should be fitted with a sprinkler system throughout | more than 11 m |
| (b) | Same trigger before the 2020 amendments | 30 m |
| (c) | Top-storey height at which flats should be served by more than one common stair | 18 m or more |
| (c) | Date the multi-stair changes take effect | 30 September 2026 |

1. DOCUMENT STATE RELIED ON
Consolidated text: Approved Document B (Fire safety) Volume 1: Dwellings, The Building Regulations 2010, 2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendments, for use in England (GOV.UK online version; the 2026 consolidated file also carries the forthcoming 2029 amendments).
Amendment booklets relied on: May 2020 amendments; March 2024 circular and Notice of Approval (multi-stair recommendation, coming into force 30 September 2026); September 2026 amendment booklet ('2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022 and 2025 amendments — taking effect on 30 September 2026').
Note on scope: the 2029 amendments reproduced in the consolidated file take effect on 2 September 2029 and are NOT part of the state asked about; they are excluded from all answers below.
Note on status: ADB is guidance approved under section 6 of the Building Act 1984. Its recommendations use 'should'. Following them is not itself a statutory duty, but they are the normal means of demonstrating compliance with the relevant requirement of Schedule 1 to the Building Regulations 2010; a designer departing from them must show compliance by other means.

2. ASK (a) — SPRINKLER TRIGGER, CURRENT
Paragraph 7.4 (Section 7: Compartmentation/sprinklers – flats; guidance relevant to Requirement B3), as substituted by the May 2020 amendments and carried forward unchanged through the 2022, 2025 and 2026 amendments:

'7.4 Blocks of flats with a top storey more than 11m above ground level (see Diagram D6) should be fitted with a sprinkler system throughout the building in accordance with Appendix E.
NOTE: Sprinklers should be provided within the individual flats, they do not need to be provided in the common areas such as stairs, corridors or landings when [these are fire sterile].'

Answer: 11 m — the obligation is engaged where the top storey is MORE THAN 11 m above ground level. At exactly 11.00 m the paragraph is not engaged; at 11.01 m it is.
Related points that belong with the answer:
- 'Throughout the building' is qualified by the NOTE: sprinkler provision is within the individual flats; common areas (stairs, corridors, landings) need not be sprinklered where they are fire sterile.
- Appendix E is unchanged: sprinkler systems in residential blocks of flats to BS 9251, or BS EN 12845 where outside the scope of BS 9251.
- The same 11 m threshold is used in the 2020 amendments for the new wayfinding-signage recommendation (floor identification and flat indication signage) and, from the 2022 amendments, for secure information boxes; evacuation alert systems use 18 m. These are separate recommendations and should not be conflated with the sprinkler trigger.

3. ASK (b) — SPRINKLER TRIGGER BEFORE THE 2020 AMENDMENTS
Original 2019 edition of ADB Volume 1 (i.e. as published before the May 2020 amendment booklet was incorporated): paragraph 7.4 set the trigger at a top storey more than 30 m above ground level.
The May 2020 amendment booklet states the change in its own words: 'a. Sprinklers: A reduction in the trigger height from 30m to 11m.'
Answer: 30 m (top storey more than 30 m above ground level).
Effective date of that change: 26 November 2020 ('The changes highlighted in this amendment booklet take effect on 26 November 2020 for use in England').
Transitional provision for that change: the 2019 edition continues to apply where a building notice or initial notice had been given, or full plans deposited, before 26 November 2020 and the building work (a) started before that day, or (b) started before 29 January 2021. A project caught by that saving is still legitimately designed to the 30 m trigger.

4. ASK (c) — MORE THAN ONE COMMON STAIR, AND ITS EFFECTIVE DATE
Guidance introduced by the 2026 amendments, in Section 3 (Means of escape – flats; Requirement B1). The amendment booklet states the change as: 'A new recommendation for more than one common stair to be provided in blocks of flats with a storey 18m or more in height.' The March 2024 circular says the same: 'a new recommendation for more than one common stair to be provided in blocks of flats with a storey 18m or more in height.'
The same amendments replace paragraph 3.27, which now frames when a single escape route from the flat entrance door is acceptable — including, for a flat on a storey served by a single common stair, the requirement that every flat be separated from that stair by a protected lobby or common protected corridor (see Diagram 3.7). In other words, the single-stair case is retained below the threshold subject to those conditions; at and above the threshold the design should provide more than one common stair.
Answer on height: 18 m. Note the drafting difference, which matters at the boundary: the stair recommendation reads 'a storey 18m or more in height' — INCLUSIVE at 18.00 m — whereas the sprinkler paragraph reads 'more than 11m' — EXCLUSIVE at 11.00 m. Do not harmonise the two.
Answer on date: the changes take effect on 30 September 2026 ('The changes highlighted in this amendment booklet take effect on 30 September 2026 for use in England'; the Notice of Approval states 'The approval takes effect on 30 September 2026').
Transitional provision: the 2019 edition incorporating the 2020, 2022 and 2025 amendments continues to apply where a building notice or initial notice has been given, or a building control approval application with full plans made, before 30 September 2026, and the work is sufficiently progressed before 30 March 2028. Those projects are not required to adopt the multi-stair recommendation.
Also in the same 2026 amendments (for completeness, not asked): building design provisions to support the use of evacuation lifts in blocks of flats.

5. MEASUREMENT CONVENTION AND BOUNDARY CASES
Both triggers are expressed as a height of storey above ground level; the sprinkler paragraph cross-refers to Diagram D6 for the measurement. Apply the height as the height of the relevant storey floor above ground level (not to roof level), taken at the lowest ground level adjoining the building on the side where the ground is lowest — i.e. the convention used in ADB for 'height above ground level' on sloping sites. Where a site slopes, the measurement side is the one that produces the greatest height and therefore governs. (Diagram D6 itself should be read in the consolidated volume for the graphical definition before it is relied on in a site-specific design; the text of Diagram D6 is not reproduced in the extracts above.)
Worked boundaries, consistent with the values stated above:
- Top storey floor at 10.9 m: no sprinkler recommendation; single common stair acceptable.
- Top storey floor at exactly 11.0 m: no sprinkler recommendation ('more than 11m'); single common stair acceptable.
- Top storey floor at 11.1 m: sprinkler system throughout (within flats) recommended; single common stair still acceptable in principle, subject to the paragraph 3.27 conditions.
- Top storey floor at 17.9 m: sprinklers recommended; single common stair acceptable.
- Top storey floor at exactly 18.0 m: sprinklers recommended AND more than one common stair recommended ('18m or more').
The 18 m stair figure being above the 11 m sprinkler figure is internally consistent: the band 11 m to under 18 m is deliberately a sprinklered single-stair band.

6. DISTINCTIONS A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK BEFORE RELYING ON THIS
- Guidance vs requirement: the 11 m sprinkler figure and the 18 m stair figure are ADB guidance ('should'), not free-standing statutory thresholds. Separately, the Building Safety Act 2022 higher-risk-building regime uses 18 m or 7 storeys as its own trigger for a different purpose (design/construction and in-occupation regime). The coincidence of 18 m is not evidence that one is the other; do not cite the HRB definition as the source of the ADB stair recommendation.
- Version discipline: 'currently published' at the date of this answer includes the 2026 amendments in force from 30 September 2026. A project with a pre-30 September 2026 notice or full plans application is governed by the 2020/2022/2025 text, under which there is no 18 m multi-stair recommendation — for that project the answer to ask (c) would be 'no such recommendation', not '18 m'.
- The 2025 amendments (Regulation 38/fire safety information; removal of national classes for reaction to fire and roofs) do not alter either the 11 m sprinkler trigger or the 18 m stair recommendation.
- The 2020 amendment's change to Table B4 (minimum periods of fire resistance) follows from the sprinkler change: a block of flats without a sprinkler system above 11 m is not permitted if the ADB guidance is followed.

7. SOURCE AUDIT TRAIL
- Paragraph 7.4 wording and '30m to 11m' reduction: ADB Vol 1 May 2020 amendments booklet; repeated in the consolidated volume's 'Main changes made by the 2020 amendments'.
- 26 November 2020 effective date and the 29 January 2021 transitional cut-off: May 2020 circular letter and amendment booklet introduction.
- 18 m multi-stair recommendation and 30 September 2026 effective date: March 2024 circular (including Notice of Approval) and the September 2026 amendment booklet; 'Main changes made by the 2026 amendments' in the consolidated volume.
- 30 March 2028 transitional progress date: Notice of Approval, Annex A to the March 2024 circular.
- 2029 amendments excluded as not in force until 2 September 2029: consolidated volume's 'Changes made by the 2029 amendments'.

interval, if used.

verdict.summary:
TRAFFIC ENGINEERING RESPONSE — MUTCD Pedestrian Interval Timing (Buffer Interval and Pedestrian Clearance Time)

Answers
-------
1. Minimum buffer interval (steady UPRAISED HAND) after the pedestrian change interval, before release of a conflicting vehicular movement — MUTCD 11th Edition (December 2023), Section 4I.06, Paragraph 4 (Standard): 2 seconds.
2. Default walking speed for sizing pedestrian clearance time — Section 4I.06 (pedestrian clearance time calculation, Paragraphs 7-16), with the adjustment provision in Paragraph 10: 3.5 feet per second.
3. Buffer interval minimum in the 2009 MUTCD — Section 4E.06, Paragraph 4 (Standard): 3 seconds. (Section 4E.06 in the 2009 edition is the predecessor of Section 4I.06 in the 11th Edition; the 2009 value was not changed by Revisions 1 or 2.)

So the buffer minimum was reduced from 3 seconds (2009) to 2 seconds (11th Edition, 2023). The default walking speed did not change between the two editions.

1. Buffer interval — 11th Edition, Section 4I.06, Paragraph 4 (Standard)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Verbatim: "A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16 of this Section). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used."
Source: MUTCD 11th Edition, December 2023, Part 4, Chapter 4I, Section 4I.06, page 722 (FHWA; mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/11th_Edition/mutcd11theditionhl.pdf; duplicate text at highways.dot.gov/media/111811). Corroborated by Figure 4I-4, "Pedestrian Intervals," which annotates the buffer interval as "2 seconds MIN." (page 724).

Engineering notes on the 2-second buffer, all from the same paragraph and figure:
- It is a Standard (shall), not Guidance. It is a floor, not a target.
- It is a minimum measured from the end of the flashing UPRAISED HAND to the first instant a conflicting vehicular movement may be released. In practice the buffer is normally absorbed by the beginning of the associated yellow change interval and/or red clearance interval (Figure 4I-4 shows three permitted relationships: Yellow Change Interval = Buffer Interval; part of Yellow + Red Clearance = Buffer Interval; Red Clearance Interval = Buffer Interval).
- The buffer may count toward the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or may begin after the calculated pedestrian clearance time has ended (Figure 4I-4 note ***). It is not an add-on that is automatically stacked on top of the clearance time.
- The buffer shall always be provided and displayed (Figure 4I-4 note ***), and shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if a red clearance interval is used.
- Constraint to hold in every timing plan: t(pedestrian change interval) + t(buffer) >= calculated pedestrian clearance time, with t(buffer) >= 2.0 s.

2. Default walking speed — 3.5 feet per second
----------------------------------------------
The pedestrian clearance time is the crossing distance divided by the assumed walking speed, and the default speed in Section 4I.06 is 3.5 ft/s. The 11th Edition text in hand states the downward-adjustment provision in Paragraph 10 (Guidance): "Where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 feet per second, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time." That clause defines 3.5 ft/s as the reference speed and makes any lower value a documented engineering judgment.

Application rules that accompany the 3.5 ft/s default:
- 3.5 ft/s is the default; it is not a mandate to use 3.5 ft/s where the pedestrian population warrants otherwise. Use a lower speed (commonly 3.0 ft/s or lower) where elderly pedestrians, children, or wheelchair users routinely use the crosswalk, and record the basis.
- Measure crossing distance from the curb or shoulder to the far curb or shoulder along the crosswalk line (the traveled-way width plus any portion of the crosswalk outside the traveled way that the pedestrian must traverse), consistent with the clearance-time definition in 4I.06.
- Walking speed applies to the pedestrian clearance time only. It does not set the walk interval: the walk interval should be at least 7 seconds (Paragraph 11, Guidance), and may be as short as 4 seconds where pedestrian volumes and characteristics do not require 7 seconds (Paragraph 12, Option).
- For a pedestrian signal head with no concurrent vehicular phase, Paragraph 7 (Guidance, Section 4I.07) directs that the flashing UPRAISED HAND be set approximately 4 seconds less than the required pedestrian clearance time, with an additional steady-UPRAISED-HAND clearance interval before the conflicting vehicular phase begins — the mechanism by which the buffer is created in that configuration.
- Countdown displays run only during the pedestrian change interval and go dark at zero; they do not run during the walk interval or during a concurrent vehicular phase's red clearance interval ending at or after the pedestrian phase (Section 4I.07, Paragraphs 5-6).

Citation caveat, stated so the reader can verify: the verbatim sentence naming 3.5 ft/s as the speed for the clearance-time calculation sits in the calculation Guidance paragraphs (7-9) of Section 4I.06; the excerpt in hand carries Paragraph 10's "slower than 3.5 feet per second" clause, which fixes 3.5 ft/s as the default. The value is not in doubt; the paragraph number to cite for the calculation itself should be confirmed against the printed page 722-724 when the citation goes into a design document.

3. 2009 MUTCD buffer minimum — 3 seconds
---------------------------------------
Verbatim (2009 MUTCD, Section 4E.06, Paragraph 4, Standard): "A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 3 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used."
Source: MUTCD 2009 Edition, December 2009, Part 4, Section 4E.06, pages 499-500 (mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/2009/part4.pdf). Corroborated by Figure 4E-2, "Pedestrian Intervals," annotated "3 seconds MIN." (page 499), and by the 2009 MUTCD Revision 2 compliance table, which lists under Section 4E.06: "New requirement in the 2009 MUTCD that the pedestrian change interval shall not extend into the red clearance interval and shall be followed by a buffer interval of at least 3 seconds (see Paragraph 4)" (mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/2009r1r2/mutcd2009r2pages.pdf).

Edition/version scope: the 3-second value is the original 2009 text and is unchanged by Revisions 1 and 2 — Revision 2 only attached a compliance date to the requirement. The 2009 structure (Section 4E.06, Figure 4E-2) maps to the 11th Edition structure (Section 4I.06, Figure 4I-4).

Side-by-side summary
--------------------
Item | 2009 MUTCD (Sec. 4E.06) | 11th Ed., Dec 2023 (Sec. 4I.06)
Buffer interval, minimum | 3 s (Para. 4, Standard; Fig. 4E-2) | 2 s (Para. 4, Standard; Fig. 4I-4)
Default walking speed for pedestrian clearance time | 3.5 ft/s | 3.5 ft/s
Walk interval, minimum (for reference) | 7 s should; 4 s option | 7 s should (Para. 11); 4 s option (Para. 12)
Governing constraint | change interval + buffer >= calculated PCT | change interval + buffer >= calculated PCT

Worked timing check (illustrative, to show the constraints are applied consistently)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Crosswalk crossing distance 60 ft; default 3.5 ft/s assumed; no documented need for a lower speed.
- Calculated pedestrian clearance time = 60 / 3.5 = 17.1 s.
- Set pedestrian change interval (flashing UPRAISED HAND) = 16 s; buffer interval = 2 s.
- Check sum: 16 + 2 = 18 s >= 17.1 s — satisfies 4I.06 Para. 4.
- Check buffer minimum: 2 s >= 2 s — satisfies 4I.06 Para. 4.
- Walk interval: 7 s (minimum per Guidance; 4 s only if volumes/characteristics permit).
- Place the 2-second buffer within the leading portion of the associated yellow change interval and/or red clearance interval; the buffer shall not begin later than the start of the red clearance interval.
- If the same crosswalk were timed under the 2009 edition, the buffer would be 3 s and the change interval could be reduced to 15 s to hold the same 18 s total clearance sum.

Conditions the requester should be aware of
-------------------------------------------
- Jurisdiction: 2 s is the FHWA 11th Edition value. The California MUTCD 2026 Edition (FHWA's 2023 edition as amended for California) carries the same 2-second Standard and the same Figure 4I-4 "2 seconds MIN.," so California does not diverge on this point. Other state MUTCD supplements must be checked individually; a state may impose a longer buffer (some retain 3 s), and the more restrictive adopted value governs the design.
- Statement type: both the 2-second (2023) and 3-second (2009) buffer minimums are Standards (shall). The 7-second walk interval is Guidance (should); the 4-second walk interval is an Option (may). Do not cite a Guidance value as a mandate in a design document.
- Phasing: Section 4I.06 Paragraph 4 applies to any conflicting vehicular movement being released, so the 2-second buffer floor is the same for concurrent pedestrian phasing and for exclusive/parallel phasing; the difference between configurations is where the buffer falls relative to the yellow and red clearance intervals, not its minimum length.

In the TQFP and QFN/MLF package, ADC7:6 serve as analog inputs to the A/D converter. These pins are powered

2. Overview
The ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P is a low-power CMOS 8-bit microcontroller based on the AVR
enhanced RISC architecture. By executing powerful instructions in a single clock cycle, the
ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P achieves throughputs approaching 1 MIPS per MHz allowing the system
designer to optimize power consumption versus processing speed.

2. I/O Registers within the address range 0x00 - 0x1F are directly bit-accessible using the SBI and CBI instructions. In these
registers, the value of single bits can be checked by using the SBIS and SBIC instructions.
3. Some of the Status Flags are cleared by writing a logical one to them. Note that, unlike most other AVRs, the CBI and SBI

Registers as data space using LD and ST instructions, 0x20 must be added to these addresses. The

within the 64 location reserved in Opcode for the IN and OUT instructions. For the Extended I/O space from 0x60 - 0xFF in

In the TQFP and QFN/MLF package, ADC7:6 serve as analog inputs to the A/D converter. These pins are powered

2. Overview
The ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P is a low-power CMOS 8-bit microcontroller based on the AVR
enhanced RISC architecture. By executing powerful instructions in a single clock cycle, the
ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P achieves throughputs approaching 1 MIPS per MHz allowing the system
designer to optimize power consumption versus processing speed.

2. I/O Registers within the address range 0x00 - 0x1F are directly bit-accessible using the SBI and CBI instructions. In these

verdict.summary:
BOTTOM LINE

DS40002061B (Microchip, 2020, 'ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P, Data Sheet Complete', revision B dated 09/2020) does not publish a junction-to-ambient thermal resistance for the ATmega328P in the 28-pin PDIP (package code 28P3), and it does not publish a maximum junction temperature or a total power dissipation rating. Neither figure exists anywhere in that document. Any degC/W number attributed to 'the ATmega328P datasheet' for the PDIP is coming from some other source, and should be re-sourced before it is used in a thermal calculation.

ASK-BY-ASK

Ask 1 (constraint): The controlling document is DS40002061B. The ATmega328P 28-pin PDIP ordering codes in that document are ATmega328P-PU and ATmega328P-PN, package 28P3 = 28-lead, 0.300 in wide, Plastic Dual Inline Package, industrial temperature range -40 C to +85 C, 20 MHz at 1.8-5.5 V.

Ask 2 (theta-JA, 28P3): Not specified. See 'Where the data would be, and is not' below.

Ask 3 (Tj(max) or total power dissipation): Not specified. The only temperature ceilings in the document are the Absolute Maximum Ratings entries Operating Temperature -55 C to +125 C and Storage Temperature -65 C to +150 C. The 125 C entry is an ambient/operating-temperature stress limit, not a junction-temperature limit, and must not be relabelled as Tj(max). There is no 'Power Dissipation' line and no derating curve (mW/degC) anywhere in the electrical characteristics.

WHERE THE DATA WOULD BE, AND IS NOT

The document is organised so that thermal data, if it existed, would sit in Section 29, 'Electrical Characteristics - (TA = -40 C to 85 C)', immediately under 29.1 Absolute Maximum Ratings, or in a dedicated 'Thermal Characteristics' section alongside the DC characteristics. Section 29.1 in DS40002061B contains, in full, this list:

  Operating Temperature .......................... -55 C to +125 C
  Storage Temperature ............................. -65 C to +150 C
  Voltage on any Pin except RESET with respect to Ground ... -0.5 V to VCC+0.5 V
  Voltage on RESET with respect to Ground ........ -0.5 V to +13.0 V
  Maximum Operating Voltage ...................... 6.0 V
  DC Current VCC and GND Pins .................... 200.0 mA
  DC Current on I/O pins ......................... 40.0 mA

followed by the standard NOTICE that stresses beyond these ratings may cause permanent damage and that exposure to absolute-maximum conditions for extended periods may affect reliability. CONFIRMATION PROCEDURE (5 minutes, on your own copy)

1. Open DS40002061B and search the PDF for: 'Thermal', 'theta', 'JA', 'junction', 'Junction', 'Power Dissipation', 'Rth', 'derat'. 
2. If every hit is in the general boilerplate or in a package drawing note, the finding above stands: no thermal data.
3. If your copy does contain a Thermal Characteristics table, use it, cite the page number, and ignore the planning values below - but verify the table row is for 28P3/PDIP and not for the 32A TQFP or 28M1 QFN, which are different packages on the same datasheet.
4. Do not accept values from the ATmega8, AT90S-series, ATmega328PB, or an app note as if they were from DS40002061B. Older Atmel datasheets (e.g. ATmega8, AT90S2313) did carry a 'Power Dissipation ... 1.0 W' absolute-maximum line with a derating curve; that is the most common source of the expectation that this datasheet has one. It does not.

ENGINEERING SUBSTITUTE (NOT FROM DS40002061B - label it as such in your design file)

theta-JA planning value for 28-lead 0.300 in PDIP: JEDEC JESD51 still-air, 2-layer test-board measurements for this package family typically fall in the 45-60 degC/W band, with the lower end requiring copper spreading on the lead rows. A PDIP's theta-JA is dominated by lead-frame conduction into the PCB, so the number moves with board copper; if the design is thermally tight, measure it.

Junction temperature: Tj = Ta + P_device * theta-JA, with Ta taken as the application's maximum ambient (85 C for the industrial grade).

  With core only (60 mW): delta-T = 3.6 C, Tj ~ 89 C.
Both are far below any plausible silicon limit (plastic packages of this class are qualified to 125-150 C), so the absence of a datasheet Tj(max) is not a practical barrier at normal operating points.

blocked_on.why: DS40002061B (09/2020) contains no thermal resistance data of any kind - no Thermal Characteristics section, no theta-JA / theta-JC / theta-JB table, and no per-package thermal row for the 28P3 (28-lead, 0.300 in PDIP). findings.question:
1. Under the Australian Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence that is in force on 17 November 2026, what maximum EIRP, in watts, is permitted for a 'digital modulation' radiocommunications transmitter operating in 2400-2483.5 MHz, what additional limit on radiated peak power spectral density applies to that class, and in what year was the instrument now in force made (its name carries the year)?

4. Whether 'digital modulation' limits for 2400–2483.5 MHz are split (e.g., different limits indoors/outdoors or by sub-band) — picking the wrong clause changes the answer.

verdict.summary:
REGULATORY DETERMINATION — LIPD Class Licence, digital modulation, 2400–2483.5 MHz, as at 17 November 2026

1. INSTRUMENT IN FORCE ON 17 NOVEMBER 2026

Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025 (Federal Register of Legislation ID F2025L01047).

- Made (dated) 4 September 2025; signed by Adam Suckling (Member) and Michael Brealey (General Manager), ACMA, under s 132 of the Radiocommunications Act 1992.
- Registered 5 September 2025 (authorised version F2025L01047 registered 05/09/2025).
- Commencement: clause 2 — 'This instrument commences at the start of 1 October 2025.'
- It replaces the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2015, which was due to sunset on 1 October 2025 and which the Federal Register now shows as 'No longer in force'. The ACMA LIPD class licence page (last updated 2 October 2025) names the 2025 instrument as the licence rules to follow.

Therefore on 17 November 2026 the operative instrument is the 2025 Class Licence, and the year carried in its name (and its year of making) is 2025.

2. MAXIMUM EIRP — DIGITAL MODULATION, 2400–2483.5 MHz

Schedule 1, table item 7 (columns: class / permitted operating frequency band / maximum EIRP / additional limitations):

  Item 7 — Digital modulation radiocommunications transmitters — 2400–2483.5 MHz — 4 W — See clause 43.

Maximum EIRP = 4 W (equivalently 4000 mW, 36 dBm, 6 dBW).

Notes on the row:
- There is no averaging qualifier on this row (contrast item 8, 5150–5250 MHz, '1 W, averaged over the entire transmission burst') and no elevation-dependent EIRP restriction (contrast clause 44 for item 8: 125 mW/21 dBm above 30° elevation). Neither qualifier applies at 2.4 GHz.
- The adjacent frequency-hopping rows in the same band are separate classes: item 2 (2400–2483.5 MHz, 500 mW, clause 40) and item 3 (2400–2483.5 MHz, 4 W, clause 41). A transmitter is assessed against the class into which it falls; the digital modulation answer is item 7.

3. ADDITIONAL LIMIT — RADIATED PEAK POWER SPECTRAL DENSITY

Clause 43 ('Additional limitation for table items 6, 7 and 9'):

  'A radiocommunications transmitter must not be operated if its radiated peak power spectral density is greater than 25 mW per 3 kHz.'

Applies to item 7 (2400–2483.5 MHz digital modulation) as an additional limitation additional to, and concurrent with, the 4 W maximum EIRP.

Limit: radiated peak power spectral density ≤ 25 mW per 3 kHz.

Equivalent expressions (for test-laboratory use):
- 25 mW per 3 kHz = 8.333 mW per 1 kHz = 13.98 dBm per 3 kHz.
- Per 1 MHz: 25 mW × (1000/3) = 8333 mW/MHz = 8.333 W/MHz = 39.2 dBm/MHz.

Interaction of the two limits (do not read the per-MHz figure as overriding the EIRP cap): the PSD limit is a density in a 3 kHz reference bandwidth, not a total-power ceiling. Both conditions must be met simultaneously. The EIRP cap of 4000 mW becomes the binding constraint once emission bandwidth exceeds 4000 / 8.333 ≈ 480 kHz; the PSD limit binds for narrowband emissions and narrowband components within a wideband emission.

4. OTHER CONDITIONS RELEVANT TO OPERATING UNDER THIS CLASS (non-numeric, for completeness)

- The device must meet the applicable technical standards referenced by the ACMA (Schedule 5 to the General Equipment Rules; Radiocommunications (Electromagnetic Compatibility) Standard 2017; EME Standard in Schedule 4 to the General Equipment Rules).
- Class licences give no protection from interference, and LIPD devices must not cause interference to radiocommunication services.
- Extra restrictions apply within 70 km of the Murchison Radioastronomy Observatory (radio quiet zone).

5. VERIFICATION / RESIDUAL RISK

Evidence base: F2025L01047 as made (PDF and EPUB text, legislation.gov.au, retrieved 23 November 2026); ACMA LIPD class licence page (last updated 2 October 2025); ACMA consultation and outcomes paper for the remaking (outcome published 5 September 2025); Federal Register entry for F2015L01438 showing the 2015 licence no longer in force.

Residual check for a duty-holder before relying on this: confirm on the Federal Register that the compilation of F2025L01047 in force on 17 November 2026 carries no amendment altering Schedule 1 item 7 or clause 43. An amendment would not change the year-made answer (2025) and, on the evidence available, the 4 W / 25 mW per 3 kHz figures are the long-standing 2.4 GHz digital modulation values carried forward from the 2015 licence.

6. ANSWERS

- Maximum EIRP, digital modulation, 2400–2483.5 MHz: 4 W.
- Additional radiated peak power spectral density limit: 25 mW per 3 kHz.
- Year the instrument now in force was made: 2025 (Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025, made 4 September 2025, commencing 1 October 2025).

Reaction to fire
Coming into force
The amendments bringing changes to the guidance are included in Approved Document B that takes effect on 2 March 2025.
Description of the changes
The update to guidance removes the national classification system (BS476) for reaction to fire and roofs from Approved Document B, which provides statutory guidance for fire safety in new building work.
The European Standard (BS EN), deemed more current and robust than the National Classes, will be the sole route of specification within Approved Document B for reaction to fire and roofs classifications.
Transitional

2. Whether the 2025/2026 amendments changed the sprinkler threshold (a) or the multiple-stair threshold (c), since answering 'as currently published' against the wrong amendment boundary returns a wrong figure
3. The exact metric intended by 'top storey more than what height above ground level' — the specific definition of height used in ADB (e.g. storey 18m vs 11m thresholds and floor vs ground level convention) decides which figure is the answer
4. The effective date of the amendment package that introduced the more-than-one-stair provision, which is directly asked for in (c) and cannot be assumed
